paragraphs.heading: A candidate for dark matter
paragraphs.text: WIMP stands for weakly interacting massive particle. WIMPs are hypothetical particles, put forward as one possible explanation for dark matter. They would have mass and feel gravity. They would have been made in huge numbers in the Big Bang and then grown fewer through a process called self-annihilation, driven by their weak interaction.

paragraphs.heading: What counts as a WIMP
paragraphs.text: There is no formal definition. Broadly, a WIMP is an elementary particle that feels gravity plus at least one other force, where that force is no stronger than the weak nuclear force but not zero either. Having no electromagnetic interaction with normal matter, WIMPs could not be seen by ordinary observations using light. They were proposed about ten years after the dark matter problem was set out in the 1970s.

paragraphs.heading: Heavy, slow and cold
paragraphs.text: Because they are heavy, WIMPs would move fairly slowly, which is what makes them cold dark matter. At those low speeds they could not escape each other's gravity, so they would tend to clump. Neutrinos, by contrast, are very light and fast, which makes them hot. Hot dark matter would smear out the large-scale pattern of galaxies, while simulations filled with cold dark matter produce galaxy layouts roughly like the ones we see.

paragraphs.heading: Left over from the Big Bang
paragraphs.text: In the very hot early universe, dark matter particles and their antiparticles would have been made from lighter particles and destroyed back into them. As the universe expanded and cooled, the lighter particles no longer had enough energy to make new pairs, but the destruction went on. Eventually the particles became so spread out that they stopped meeting, and their number has stayed roughly fixed since then. Working back from how much dark matter exists today, the strength of that destruction can be no larger than that of the weak interaction. If this picture is right, the dark matter particle would have the properties of a WIMP.

paragraphs.heading: The WIMP miracle
paragraphs.text: Supersymmetry, a type of extension to particle physics' Standard Model, readily predicts new particles that could serve as WIMPs, such as neutralinos and gravitinos. This apparent coincidence has been named the WIMP miracle. For many years, a stable supersymmetric partner particle has been a leading candidate. However, the Large Hadron Collider has found no evidence for supersymmetry, which casts doubt on the simplest versions of the idea.

paragraphs.heading: The search so far
paragraphs.text: Because WIMPs would interact only through gravity and the weak force, they would be extremely hard to detect. Researchers look for gamma rays, neutrinos and cosmic rays made when WIMPs annihilate in nearby galaxies and clusters. Others try to catch WIMPs hitting atomic nuclei in the laboratory, or to create them in particle colliders like CERN's Large Hadron Collider. As of 2026, none of these searches has succeeded.
